summary: Describes how to register a domain with the Network Information Center of the DDN and gives guidelines for setting up and running a domain, following the requirements of RFC 920. It recommends these guidelines for administrators of second-level domains, whose role is coordinator, manager and technician.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1032 explains how domain administrators register a domain with the DDN Network Information Center and keep its data current. It also describes the administrative and technical responsibilities of running a domain.

subtitle: A guide to registering and administering a domain in the DDN and DARPA naming system.

tldr.problem: Organizations needed guidance on registering a domain and assigning responsibility for keeping its names and name servers in order.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes administrator and technical-contact roles, naming guidance, the NIC registration questionnaire and ways to verify registered information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1032 is a guide for domain administrators and says it should be used with RFC 920. The unit metadata records its status as Unknown and lists no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Administrative and Technical Roles
sections.content:
The domain administrator coordinates domain management, handles naming assignments and ensures that the domain's data stays current. The administrator works with the organization responsible for the parent domain when registering a domain below it.

The technical and zone contact maintains the name server, resolver software and database files. The RFC defines a zone as a contiguous part of the domain tree for which a server has complete information and authority.
sections.plainLanguage: The domain administrator manages names and the relationship with the parent domain. The technical contact maintains the software and data that serve the domain.

sections.title: Naming and Local Policy
sections.content:
The memo treats domain and host name choices as local matters. It says the NIC will answer technical questions but will not arbitrate disputes over who has a right to a name.

A domain-name segment can contain up to 64 characters, but the NIC strongly advises administrators to choose names of 12 characters or fewer. The RFC also says country top-level domains should use the two-letter ISO-3166 code, with a three-letter form considered where it conflicts with a U.S. state code.
sections.plainLanguage: Organizations must settle name disputes locally before registration. The memo recommends short names, even though each segment can be longer.

sections.title: Top-Level Domain Categories
sections.content:
The guide describes the top-level domains ARPA, COM, EDU, GOV, MIL, NET and ORG, along with country domains. It gives an intended role for each of the named categories, such as companies for COM and educational institutions for EDU.

The RFC says a host should have one name regardless of which networks it connects to. Domain names should generally not contain routing information or addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide groups domains by their intended purpose, such as education, government or business. A host keeps one name even when it connects to more than one network.

sections.title: Applying and Verifying Domain Information
sections.content:
An applicant obtains the NIC questionnaire, completes it and returns it by email to the NIC hostmaster. The application includes administrative and technical contacts, the domain name, name-server information and planned name mappings. The NIC reviews it for completeness and may exchange follow-up messages before authorizing the domain.

A domain must provide at least two independent servers. Administrators can check registered information with the NIC WHOIS service or by sending an email query, and are responsible for keeping domain data current.
sections.plainLanguage: The administrator submits a completed form to the NIC and answers any follow-up questions. The domain must provide at least two independent servers and keep its registration information current.
